expedition: The Lucas Vázquez de Ayllón Expedition
sources: Gilbert J. Garraghan, S.J., "Catholic First Things in the United States," Mid-America: An Historical Review, vol. 21 (1939) | https://archive.org/details/midamericahistor21unse/ ; Catholic Church in the United States - Wikipedia | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church_in_the_United_States
notes:
This is universally recognized as the first Catholic Mass of any kind celebrated on the mainland of the United States. Because the celebrating friars belonged to the Order of Preachers (Dominicans), they naturally used their own unique liturgical format, the Dominican Rite, which had been universally mandated for all Dominican friars since the 13th century. The colony tragically collapsed after only three months due to disease, cold weather, and a slave rebellion, leading the survivors to abandon the site and return to Santo Domingo.

Per Gilbert J. Garraghan, S.J. ("Catholic First Things in the United States," Mid-America, 1939), the two Dominicans landed with Lucas Vazquez de Ayllon's expedition on or about September 29, 1526, but the exact location of the mission they founded, San Miguel de Gualdape, was never settled among early historians. Garraghan surveys three competing identifications: Lowery (Spanish Settlements, I, 166), followed by Bolton (The Spanish Borderlands, 17), placed it on the Pedee River in South Carolina -- the location used for this entry. Shea (Catholic Church in the United States, I, 107, and in Winsor's Narrative and Critical History, II, 241) instead placed it at the site of the future Jamestown, Virginia, an identification accepted with some reservation by O'Daniel and Kenny. Harrisse (Discovery of North America, 213) placed it on the lower Cape Fear River in North Carolina. Bourne (Spain in America, 140, n. 1) considered the location undeterminable with certainty. Given Shea's stature as a foundational figure in American Catholic historiography, the Virginia identification deserves real weight as an alternative to the South Carolina placement used here.

sources: HMDB | https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=120361 ; Father Jerome. "The First Bishop of Florida." The Florida Historical Quarterly 40, no. 3 (January 1962): 295–300.
notes:
In April 1528, The Spanish explorer Panfilo de Narvaez arrived here with 5 ships and 600 men in a quest for gold and power. Also with him were those who sought to spread Christianity, including eight diocesan and five Franciscan priests. One of those priests, Fr. Juan Xuarez, OFM, had received an appointment as Bishop of Florida. A few days after their arrival, Fr. Xuarez celebrated Easter Mass ashore on the morning of April 16th. After another ten days in the area which included several violent encounters with the native Tocobaga peoples. Narvaez along with half of the crew (including 5 priests) headed north on land in what would prove to be an ill-fated expedition. Eight years later in 1536, a mere four survivors made it to Mexico.

The title "Bishop of Florida" attached to Fr. Xuarez requires a caveat: he was Bishop-elect, never consecrated. Emperor Charles V, exercising the patronage privilege granted to Spain by the bulls of Pope Julius II, nominated Xuarez to the see -designated in period documents as the "Bishopric of the Palms River and La Florida" - but the Papal bulls confirming the appointment never arrived before Narváez's expedition departed. A surviving letter from Charles V to Xuarez, dated Burgos, February 15, 1528, and preserved in the Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Indiferente General, Legajo 421), addresses him as bishop-designate and authorizes him to administer diocesan revenues and act as protector of the Indians in the interim. Historians have disputed the appointment for decades — some dismissing it as legend — but the Seville letter, first published in English translation in 1962, settles the nomination itself even as it confirms Xuarez died in 1528 or shortly after without ever receiving formal consecration.

expedition: Juan de Oñate New Mexico Expedition
sources: The Spokesman Review | https://www.spokesman.com/stories/1999/nov/21/thanksgiving-could-have-been-in-april/ ; Marina B. Ochoa, "Archives of the Archdiocese of Santa Fe and 400 Years of Church History in New Mexico," U.S. Catholic Historian, vol. 16, no. 1 (Winter 1998), pp. 23-34 | https://www.jstor.org/stable/25154619
notes:
Franciscan friars erected a makeshift altar in a grove of cottonwood trees. They celebrated a high Mass of Thanksgiving on the Catholic holy day of the Ascension. 
The ceremony included the Latin Mass, the singing of the Te Deum hymn by colonists, and Onate's verbal declaration of possession of the land.
The Thanksgiving prayer uttered was: "Open the door to these heathens, establish the church altars where the body and blood of the Son of God may be offered; open to us the way to security and peace for their preservation and ours, and give to our king and to me in his royal name, peaceful possession of these kingdoms and provinces for his blessed glory. Amen"

A more elaborate, and harder to credit, description comes from Gaspar Perez de Villagra's epic poem Historia de la Nueva Mexico (1610), an account by a captain who was on the expedition -- per Marina B. Ochoa's summary of it, Villagra describes the Mass as sung inside "a graceful church, one with a nave of such a size that all the camp at once might be contained in it without crowding," with Martinez giving a celebrated sermon and a drama performed afterward. Worth taking with a grain of salt: this is an epic poem, not a plain log or diary, and a full timber-built "graceful church" at a traveling camp on the day of arrival seems unlikely on its face -- probably poetic exaggeration of the makeshift altar rather than a literal structure. Included here for completeness, not as a correction to the grove-altar description above.

notes: Per Gilbert J. Garraghan, S.J., "Catholic First Things in the United States" (Mid-America, 1939), citing Fray Zephyrin Engelhardt's The Franciscans in Arizona (1899) and H. H. Bancroft's Arizona and New Mexico, Frs. Francisco de Porras and Andrés Gutiérrez, together with lay brother Cristóbal de la Concepción, reached the Hopi ("Moqui") towns in 1628 or 1629 and became the first resident priests in what's now Arizona, founding the mission of San Bernardino at Awatovi. They baptized around 800 Hopi within a few years. Fr. Porras was later poisoned by resentful medicine men and died reciting the psalm "In te, Domine, speravi."  Engelhardt calls him "the proto-martyr of Arizona" for it. Neither source states outright that Mass was said at Awatovi, but given years of resident ministry and hundreds of baptisms there, it's a reasonable inference that Mass was among the sacraments celebrated at the mission not long after the 1628/29 arrival. This is a different claim from the site's existing Arizona entry (the 1539/40 Coronado-era entrada near Chichilticalli). Garraghan credits that earlier expedition with the first Mass said anywhere in the state, while Awatovi is the state's first fixed mission and first resident Mass. Wikipedia's article on Awatovi Ruins covers the site's later archaeology and 1700 destruction but wasn't used as a source here.

Services in what's now New Orleans go back further, though earlier records are murkier, attested mostly through letter-writing turf wars between Jesuits and Franciscans. This is specifically about the site of today's St. Louis Cathedral. Some sources cite 1718, when the first (surely simple, wooden) church was built on the site. Wikipedia's own article can't seem to make up its mind between 1718 and 1720 either.

But the first surviving sacramental record -a nuptial Mass- is 1720, and I've verified this directly against Chambon's In and Around the Old St. Louis Cathedral of New Orleans. P. 35 lists "Father Prothay Boyer, 1720, a Recollet" as the first rector, serving from the city's founding to 1788. P. 96 quotes the actual parish register entry: a marriage record from July 1, 1720, referencing banns published at a parochial Mass on June 16, 1720, signed by Boyer as "missionary and acting pastor." I also checked every 1718 mention in the book — all three refer to Bienville founding the city, none to a church or Mass. No 1718 church/Mass date turns up in this source.

So: 1718 has support elsewhere as a construction date, but 1720 is the attested date directly from the cited work, and it's what I'd list.

The Old Ursuline Convent calls Boyer the "first rector," which I take as loose phrasing rather than a claim to more precise records. They also place it in the Diocese of Quebec at the time. He was a Recollet, and within a couple years the parish was handed to the Capuchins.

sources: Wikipedia | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral_of_San_Fernando_(San_Antonio) ; Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas -- "Garza, Jose Refugio Guadalupe de la" | https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/garza-jose-refugio-guadalupe-de-la ; Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas -- "San Fernando Cathedral Parish" | https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/san-fernando-cathedral-parish
notes:
First Mass of the Mexican forces during the Texas revolution. When General Cos marched into San Antonio with hundreds of fresh Mexican permanent troops, he immediately sought to secure the loyalty of the local population. On Sunday, October 11, Cos ordered a grand military Mass at San Fernando Church. He had his soldiers form dress lines, and the Mexican flag was solemnly blessed. This Mass served a dual purpose: fulfilling Sunday obligation for the troops and sending a strict political message of Mexican sovereignty over the territory just as Texian forces began marching toward the city.

Biographical background on the celebrant, per the Texas State Historical Association's Handbook of Texas (a real academic source, not just Wikipedia): Jose Refugio Guadalupe de la Garza was born in San Antonio, November 22, 1775, and became the town's third native-born pastor, appointed parish priest of San Antonio in 1819 and arriving to take up the post in January 1820, a tenure that lasted two decades. He remained a Mexican loyalist through the revolution and was later among those ordered by Santa Anna to help dispose of and burn the bodies of the fallen Alamo defenders. He was removed from office by incoming foreign Catholic clergy in 1840, afterward serving as chaplain of the Presidial Company of the Rio Grande until his death in 1845 or 1846.

Worth noting: checked four separate Handbook of Texas entries (this one, the general San Fernando Cathedral history, the Siege of Bexar entry, and Garza's own biography) plus general web searches -- none independently confirm the specific October 11, 1835 Mass, the flag-blessing detail, or the exact date. That specific claim is still sourced to Wikipedia alone; the TSHA sources here strengthen Garza's biography and credentials but don't yet corroborate the event itself, which is why this entry remains marked inferred rather than confirmed.
